Baby & Child

Dates while breastfeeding: nutrition, safety and milk supply

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

You can usually eat dates while breastfeeding if you enjoy and tolerate them. They provide food energy and fibre, but are optional: neither milk quality nor your baby's intelligence depends on eating a particular fruit. Claims about dates increasing milk deserve a more careful look.

What dates are

Dates are the fruit of Phoenix dactylifera, a palm in the Arecaceae family cultivated for thousands of years. Fruit grows in clusters, and varieties differ in size, colour, sweetness and texture. Fresh and dried dates are foods; a large soft date is not the same portion as a small dry one.

The palm also supplies materials for baskets, mats, furniture and other products. Its fruit is eaten plain or used in bread, desserts and syrups. These uses do not establish medicinal benefits for flowers, seeds, sap or concentrated extracts.

What they contribute to your diet

Dates contain carbohydrate, including natural sugars, alongside fibre and minerals such as potassium and magnesium. Their composition varies with variety and drying. They are not a substitute for protein foods, vegetables, calcium-rich foods or a prescribed supplement.

During breastfeeding, aim for varied meals and enough food and drink for your needs. Dates chopped into porridge or plain yoghurt can be one option. You do not need a special milk-making diet, and every food you eat does not simply pass unchanged into milk.

Do dates increase breast milk?

A 2021 randomized trial included 48 mother–infant pairs, with babies aged 1–3 months. Twenty-five mothers added 10 dates daily for four weeks; 23 continued their usual diet without dates. Pump-measured milk quantity increased more in the date group, but infant nutritional status did not differ between groups.

This small, short study is a promising signal, not proof that dates reliably treat low supply, enrich milk or improve infant intelligence. Pump output is not the same as a baby's total milk intake. The study's intake is not a recommended daily dose, and its abstract alone cannot settle long-term effectiveness or safety.

Feeding support matters more than a food remedy

If you worry about milk supply, ask a midwife, lactation specialist or clinician to observe a feed and review attachment, milk transfer, feeding frequency and your baby's weight and nappies. Effective, regular milk removal supports production; a fruit cannot correct every feeding or medical difficulty.

Get prompt advice for poor feeding, fewer wet nappies than expected for age or poor weight gain. Do not postpone assessment while trying dates or stop clinically needed supplementation. A baby who is difficult to wake, struggles to breathe or has had no urine for 12 hours needs immediate emergency care.

Traditional health claims and their limits

Dates and their compounds have attracted research interest, including laboratory work on antioxidant activity. A cell, animal or concentrated-extract result cannot establish that ordinary servings treat infections, inflammation, cancer, Alzheimer's disease, diabetes, kidney failure or stones, night blindness, cough or joint and back pain.

Claims about improved memory, learning, sleep, stress, immunity, sexual function, sperm quality, fertility, skin ageing, hair regrowth or detoxification are not a reason to replace proven assessment or treatment with dates. They are also not a reliable home method of starting labour or an interchangeable substitute for oxytocin.

Energy, constipation, iron and bone health

Dates can contribute energy and fibre, which may help as part of an overall bowel-care plan. Increase fibre gradually and drink according to your needs. Persistent constipation, marked tiredness or hair loss can have several causes and should not automatically be attributed to diet or treated with a single food.

Suspected iron-deficiency anaemia needs assessment and appropriate treatment; dates do not replace prescribed iron. Likewise, their mineral content does not make them a sufficient calcium source or a proven prevention for osteoporosis. Include suitable calcium-rich foods and discuss supplements when indicated.

Sugar, portions and practical safety

Natural sugars still count towards carbohydrate intake. If you have diabetes, fit dates into your individualized meal plan rather than assuming they lower blood glucose or banning all fruit. Size and preparation matter: date syrup, sweetened drinks and desserts are different from a portion of whole fruit.

Dried fruit sticks to teeth, so keep it to mealtimes rather than frequent nibbling and maintain dental care. Choose sound fruit, remove stones before eating and follow storage instructions. Large or suddenly increased amounts can cause digestive discomfort; there is no universal breastfeeding portion everyone must eat.

Possible reactions and when to seek care

Dates are generally compatible with breastfeeding as an ordinary food, unless you have an allergy or an individual dietary restriction. Concentrated remedies and supplements require separate checks. Mouth ulcers, acne or headaches are not inevitable effects in everyone and persistent symptoms need assessment rather than a body-temperament label.

Seek emergency help for throat or tongue swelling, breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness after food; use prescribed emergency allergy medicine as instructed. For a suspected milder allergy, stop the suspected food and obtain clinical advice. Avoid broad maternal food exclusions for infant symptoms without professional support.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Choose varied meals; include dates only if you enjoy them and they fit your dietary needs.

Ask for an observed feed and growth review if supply is a concern; do not delay needed supplementation or treatment.

Discuss portions, allergies, restrictions and concentrated products with your clinician when relevant.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you note foods, feeding questions and symptoms for appointments. It cannot measure milk transfer, diagnose low supply or allergy, assess infant hydration or prescribe supplements. Feeding concerns and warning signs need clinical care regardless of app entries.

When to seek help

Get emergency help for breathing difficulty, throat or tongue swelling, fainting or loss of consciousness after food. A baby who is difficult to wake, struggles to breathe or has no urine for 12 hours needs immediate emergency care. Poor feeding, fewer wet nappies or poor growth need prompt professional advice. Do not use dates to replace prescribed treatment or clinically needed feeds.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Dates are an optional food within a varied breastfeeding diet, not a requirement for good milk.
  • One small four-week trial suggests a possible milk-volume effect; infant nutritional status did not improve.
  • Poor feeding, wet-nappy or growth concerns need feeding assessment rather than a food trial.
  • Consider carbohydrate portions, dental care, individual restrictions and digestive tolerance.
  • Breathing difficulty, throat swelling or loss of consciousness needs emergency help.

Frequently asked questions

Are traditional benefits of dates proven?

Food nutrients and laboratory findings do not establish the wide range of claimed disease treatments. Enjoy dates as food without substituting them for medical care.

What benefits can dates offer while breastfeeding?

They provide energy, fibre and some minerals. A small trial found greater pump-measured milk quantity, but no difference in infant nutritional status; this does not establish improved intelligence or richer milk.

Are dates safe while breastfeeding?

Usually, as an ordinary food you tolerate. Allergy, diabetes, kidney-related dietary restrictions or other individual conditions may require tailored advice. Extracts and supplements are separate products.

What side effects can occur?

Large portions may cause digestive discomfort and sticky dried fruit can affect teeth. Natural sugars matter for carbohydrate planning. Allergy is possible; acne, ulcers and headaches are not guaranteed reactions.

Should I eat 10 dates every day for milk supply?

No standard dose is established. Ten daily was the intake in one short trial, not a prescription. Date size varies and milk-supply concerns need assessment.

Can dates replace iron or calcium treatment?

No. Suspected anaemia needs testing and appropriate treatment, and bone health requires adequate overall nutrition. Keep prescribed medicines and discuss supplements with your clinician.

Can I eat dates if I have diabetes?

Often yes within your individual carbohydrate plan. Consider the portion, date size and other ingredients; natural sugar is still carbohydrate and dates do not cure diabetes.

When should feeding concerns be urgent?

Seek prompt help for poor feeding, reduced wet nappies or poor growth. Difficulty waking, breathing difficulty or no urine for 12 hours in a baby requires immediate emergency care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
